Summary:

The computational rules through which the brain prioritizes experiences for storage in episodic memory are an active area of research, and one where there has been considerable disagreement in the literature. Here Rouhani and Niv rectify seemingly contradictory results from previous studies by showing that effects of rewarding and surprising outcomes on memory occur at different times in the course of a decision task, and they go on to link them to longstanding learning signals that have played instrumental roles in behavioral psychology.

Reviewers agreed that the findings are timely and interesting. There were extensive discussions among reviewers about critical aspects of the current task design that may make it difficult to relate the current results to previous findings. Specifically, the instructions given to participants encourage explicitly evaluating the stimuli and remembering them for later use. The concern is that even though the authors claim to resolve conflicting findings about modulators of memory, this is difficult to achieve with the current design because it is too different from existing work on reward-modulated memory. To better integrate the current findings with previous work, it would be important to replicate experiment 2 using instructions that do not encourage explicit memorization and allow for more incidental memory encoding.

Essential revisions:

1) There is a qualitative distinction between the current intentional encoding-for-later-use task and the overwhelmingly more common incidental memory tasks that have been used for decades, and to which the authors are trying to connect to. In general, even though the authors claim to resolve some apparently contradictory predictions about modulators of memory, they cannot do that with this design because it is too different from existing work on reward-modulated memory. Their instructed design makes it more akin to the reward-motivated memory work started by Adcock et al., 2006, where participants were incentivized to remember pictures based on cued value. The closest parallel to the current report is the work by Murty et al., 2016; see their Table 1, Experiment 3). There, participants were instructed to remember stimuli for later in the experiment (although remembering associated outcomes was not explicitly instructed). While not the focus of their study, they report no effect of reward on later memory. The current results could be part of the start of a different research direction (building on null findings from Murty et al.) on the relationship between strategic encoding-for-later-use, reward, and memory. It is unclear whether that direction would shed light on how memory is actually used outside of the lab, and such a re-framing would require a very significant re-framing of the current manuscript. Focusing on what the instructed encoding of pictures and outcomes does to memory, what do the results suggest? In these situations, it may be a rational strategy to pay greater attention to and prioritize the encoding of highly variant outcomes (surprising positive and negative deviations from expectations) if participants are trying to remember these associations for later choices. Thus, the reported modulation of memory by unsigned prediction error may be an expected consequence of instructing participants to remember associations between pictures and outcomes. To overcome these issues, reviewers would like to see an exact replication of experiment 2 without explicit instructions to memorize the items. Given data are collected online, this should be possible despite potential lab closings due to COVID-19.

2) Reviewers were not completely convinced by the model-fitting, although they felt it plays a relatively minor role for the current study, as it is unclear whether the Mackintosh signal needs to affect decision making behavior in order to affect longer term memory storage. Regardless, the model selection would be more convincing if it included the following additional information: 1) a confusion matrix demonstrating that at least one of the model comparison tools used can reliably recover the correct model, 2) posterior predictive checks showing that the winning model can capture basic learning curves, and 3) parameter fits from the winning model that make clear systematic contributions of the Mackintosh and Pearce Hall terms to positive (or negative) adjustments to the learning rate. If there is no systematic sign for Mackintosh parameter, it would be useful to know whether the sign of fits per subject corresponds to memory difference for images on positive versus negative RPE trials.

3) An additional concern is whether the proposed cue RPE modulator is actually specific to the cue RPE. On each trial, there are two factors that are highly correlated with cue RPE: the estimated value and the feedback value. In the current data, the benefit of including the Mackintosh effect on the model fits suggests that the effect comes on after values begin to be differentiated, supporting a cue RPE influence. However, an alternative model where the effect exists already at the start of learning was not evaluated. The task is very short – there are only 30 trials (15 per category) in Experiment 2. It is reasonable to assume that some initial period is necessary for participants to adjust to the task requirements / establish a “task-set” guiding their behavior, which here could cover a meaningful proportion of trials. Even if fits are better for a delayed onset of the Mackintosh effect, this could just be due to initial task adjustment adding noise to initial trials. If the participants engaged in an additional round of learning (over a new set of two types of stimuli), or if there was an extended practice session before the onset of the currently unfamiliar task, the authors could determine whether their observed result is actually due to acquisition of a cue value (leading to cue RPEs). If the observed effect is instead related to the relative estimated value or relative feedback magnitude, these would have a rapid influence on learning (once a few events are observed to roughly determine the feedback range, similar to scaling effects on dopamine RPEs). Following from this, if the feedback value is driving the observed effect, this might be due to an influence of memory for specific preceding feedback value. Basing next-trial estimates on memory for preceding trial feedback would lead to a higher estimated learning rate. This memory effect could be due to short-term working memory, given the rapid trial repetition (Collins et al.), or episodic memory.

claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing the two memory instruction conditions.

claims.claim: Participants' estimates were, on average, lower during the pandemic than before, demonstrating more pessimistic expectations overall.
claims.source: Interestingly, participants' estimates, and thus expectations for reward, were, on average, lower during the pandemic than before, demonstrating more pessimistic expectations overall (β = −1.17, t = −2.65, p=0.008).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing data collected during different time periods.

claims.claim: The RW-PH-M-D model (including Pearce-Hall, Mackintosh, and decay components) predicted participant value estimates best in Experiment 2.
claims.source: The model that included all three tested modulators of learning rate—an unsigned RPE at outcome (Pearce-Hall component), a signed RPE at cue (Mackintosh component), and an exponential decay—predicted participant value estimates best (Figure 2B,C,E, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by model comparison using likelihood-ratio tests.

claims.claim: In the high-variance condition, there was a lower average memory score for cue events and a higher average memory score for outcome events, compared to the low-variance condition.
claims.source: We found an interaction of cue versus outcome memory by variance condition, such that in the high-variance condition, there was a lower average memory score for cue events, and a higher average memory score for outcome events, compared to the low-variance condition (μ high-variance cue memory = 6.44, μ low-variance cue memory = 6.57, μ high-variance outcome memory = 5.79, μ low-variance outcome memory = 5.54; mixed-effects linear regression: β = −0.37, t = −2.78, p=0.005).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data across variance conditions.

claims.claim: There was a significant difference in memory for outcome events between high and low variance conditions.
claims.source: Within the interaction, there was a significant difference in memory for outcome events (β = −0.25, t = −2.09, p=0.04) but not for cue events (β = 0.12, t = 1.41, p=0.16).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, cue memory did not change relative to outcome memory throughout learning.
claims.source: In line with our predictions, in Experiment 1, we did not find cue memory to change relative to outcome memory throughout learning (mixed-effects linear regression, memory as a function of the interaction between event type (cue or outcome) and learning trial, β = 0.009, t = 0.13, p=0.90; Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data and reference to figure.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, memory for cue events improved throughout the experiment, relative to memory for outcome events, in both difficulty conditions.
claims.source: whereas in Experiment 2, memory for cue events improved throughout the experiment, relative to memory for outcome events, in both difficulty conditions (interaction between event type and learning trial, 40¢−60¢ condition: β = −0.24, t = −3.76, p<0.001; 20¢−80¢ condition: β = −0.20, t = −3.29, p<0.001; Figure 3B–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data and reference to figures.

claims.claim: The increase in cue memory as a function of learning was not found in the 40¢−60¢ learning condition of the incidental memory version.
claims.source: We did not find the increase in cue memory as a function of learning in the 40¢−60¢ learning condition (interaction between event type and learning trial: β = 0.07, t = 1.11, p=0.27; three-way interaction between event type, instructed-incidental memory and learning trial β = 0.31, t = 3.39, p<0.001; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data and reference to figure.

claims.claim: The increase in cue memory was replicated in the 20¢−80¢ condition of the incidental memory version.
claims.source: However, we did replicate the increase in cue memory in the 20¢−80¢ condition (interaction between event type and learning trial: β = −0.17, t = −2.79, p=0.005; three-way interaction between event type, instructed-incidental memory and learning trial: β = 0.04, t = 0.41, p=0.68; Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data and reference to figure.

claims.claim: Better individual learning predicted a greater increase in memory for cue events but not for outcome events.
claims.source: Overall, better individual learning predicted a greater increase in memory for cue events (linear regression: β = 0.02, t = 3.07, p=0.002), but not for outcome events (β = 0.001, t = 0.24, p=0.81; interaction between event type and learning performance: β = −0.01, t = −2.29, p=0.02).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of individual differences in learning and memory.

claims.claim: The relationship between learning performance and increase in cue memory was stronger in the incidental memory task than in the instructed one.
claims.source: This relationship was stronger in the incidental memory task (β = 0.02, t = 3.61, p<0.001; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) than in the instructed one (β = −0.004, t = −0.61, p=0.55, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; interaction between instructed-incidental memory and learning performance: β = 0.03, t = 2.61, p=0.009)
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing the two memory instruction conditions.

claims.claim: Unsigned outcome RPEs enhanced memory for outcome images in all experiments.
claims.source: In all experiments, we found that unsigned outcome RPEs enhanced memory for outcome images (outcome memory as a function of |outcome RPE|, Experiment 1: M = 0.14, HDI [0.06, 0.23], β = 0.19, t = 3.51, p<0.001, Figure 4A; Experiment 2 - instructed memory: M = 0.14, HDI [0.05, 0.23], β = 0.09, t = 2.59, p=0.009, Figure 4D; Experiment 2 - incidental memory: M = 0.13, HDI [0.06, 0.19], β = 0.11, t = 3.01, p=0.003, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression across all experiments.

claims.claim: Unsigned outcome RPEs due to reward variance and change points separately increased memory for outcome images in Experiment 1.
claims.source: We found separate effects of RPEs due only to reward variance and those due to change points on increasing memory for outcome images (outcome memory as a function of variance RPEs: β = 0.14, t = 2.38, p=0.02; outcome memory as a function of change-point RPEs: β = 0.24, t = 2.08, p=0.04).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis separating different sources of unsigned RPEs.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, unsigned outcome RPEs boosted memory for cue images from that same trial, with a median parameter estimate half the size of that for outcome images.
claims.source: In Experiment 1, we also found unsigned outcome RPEs to boost memory for cue images from that same trial, but with a median parameter estimate half the size of that for outcome images (cue memory as a function of |outcome RPE|: M = 0.08, HDI [−0.01, 0.16], β = 0.10, t = 2.29, p=0.02, Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, unsigned outcome RPE enhanced memory only for outcome images, not for cue images.
claims.source: We did not find this effect in any of the conditions of Experiment 2, where unsigned outcome RPE enhanced memory only for outcome images (Experiment 2 - instructed memory, cue memory as a function of |outcome RPE|: M = −0.02, HDI [−0.11, 0.06], β = −0.01, t = −0.46, p=0.64, interaction between event type (cue or outcome event) and |outcome RPE|: β = 0.09, t = 2.06, p=0.04; Experiment 2 - incidental memory, cue memory as a function of |outcome RPE|: M = −0.004, HDI [−0.07, 0.07], β = 0.006, t = 0.20, p=0.84, interaction between event type and |outcome RPE|: β = 0.09, t = 1.98, p=0.05, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claims.claim: Signed outcome RPEs did not influence memory for cue or outcome images in either experiment.
claims.source: As expected based on previous work (Rouhani et al., 2018), we did not find any influence of signed outcome RPEs on memory for cue or outcome images in either experiment (Figure 4B,F; cue memory as a function of signed outcome RPE, Experiment 1: M = −0.02, HDI [−0.11, 0.06], β = −0.05, t = −1.04, p=0.30; Experiment 2 - instructed memory, M = 0.002, HDI [−0.07, 0.07], β = −0.02, t = −0.66, p=0.51; Experiment 2 - incidental memory, M = −0.01, HDI [−0.08, 0.05], β = −0.003, t = −0.08, p=0.93; outcome memory as a function of signed outcome RPE, Experiment 1: M = −0.0007, HDI [−0.09, 0.08], β = −0.004, t = −0.07, p=0.95; Experiment 2 - instructed memory, M = −0.03, HDI [−0.10, 0.03], β = −0.05, t = −1.46, p=0.15; Experiment 2 - incidental memory, M = −0.05, HDI [−0.11, 0.02], β = −0.06, t = −1.61, p=0.11).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression across experiments, and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, signed cue RPEs boosted memory for both cue and outcome events.
claims.source: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, we found that signed cue RPEs (i.e. the signed difference between the participant-reported value of the current cue and the most-recently reported value of the alternative cue) boosted memory for both cue and outcome events, such that memory of higher (relative) value scenes was better than that for lower (relative) value scenes (cue memory as a function of signed cue RPE: M = 0.08, HDI [0.01, 0.15], β = 0.08, t = 2.64, p=0.008; outcome memory as a function of signed cue RPE: M = 0.06, HDI [−0.01, 0.12], β = 0.07, t = 2.23, p=0.03; Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claims.claim: In the incidental memory version of Experiment 2, signed cue RPE enhanced memory for cue images but not outcome images.
claims.source: In the incidental version, we replicated the effect of cue RPE on memory for cue images, but not on memory for outcome images (cue memory as a function of signed cue RPE: M = 0.10, HDI [0.04, 0.17], β = 0.09, t = 3.04, p=0.002; outcome memory as a function of signed cue RPE: M = 0.03, HDI [−0.04, 0.09], β = 0.03, t = 0.80, p=0.42; Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claims.claim: Unsigned cue RPE enhanced overall memory in the instructed memory version of Experiment 2.
claims.source: We found a separate effect of unsigned cue RPE on memory, such that the more participants had separated the values of the two scene categories (i.e. the more they had learned), the better their memory for scene images. This effect was evident in overall memory in the instructed memory version of Experiment 2 (memory as a function of |cue RPE|: β = 0.07, t = 2.49, p=0.01)
claims.evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis.

claims.claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, the effects of unsigned cue RPE on cue and outcome memory separately were only trending to significance.
claims.source: however, when quantifying the effect for cue and outcome memory separately, each of them was only trending to significance (cue memory as a function of |cue RPE|: M = 0.09, HDI [0.01, 0.16], β = 0.07, t = 1.88, p=0.06; outcome memory as a function of |cue RPE|: M = 0.06, HDI [−0.01, 0.13], β = 0.08, t = 1.82, p=0.07; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claims.claim: In the incidental memory version of Experiment 2, unsigned cue RPEs significantly increased memory for cue images but not outcome images.
claims.source: In the incidental version of Experiment 2, unsigned cue RPEs significantly increased memory for cue images (cue memory as a function of |cue RPE|: M = 0.12, HDI [0.05, 0.18], β = 0.10, t = 2.93, p=0.003), but not outcome images (outcome memory as a function of |cue RPE|: M = 0.02, HDI [−0.05, 0.08], β = 0.01, t = 0.30, p=0.76; interaction between event type and |cue RPE|: β = −0.10, t = −2.22, p=0.03; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claims.claim: Reward outcome did not predict memory in any of the experiments.
claims.source: We did not find reward outcome, in of itself or in an interaction with cue or outcome event, to predict memory in any of the experiments (memory as a function of reward outcome, Experiment 1: β = −0.03, t = −0.68, p=0.50, interaction between event type and reward outcome: β = 0.07, t = 1.07, p=0.29; Experiment 2 - instructed memory: β = 0.03, t = 0.91, p=0.36, interaction between event type and reward outcome: β = 0.02, t = 0.55, p=0.58; Experiment 2 - incidental memory: β = 0.05, t = 1.51, p=0.13, interaction between event type and reward outcome: β = −0.04, t = −0.98, p=0.33).
claims.evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis across all experiments.

claims.claim: Participant value estimates did not predict memory in Experiment 1.
claims.source: When testing the effect of participant value estimates on memory, we similarly did not find participant value estimates, in of themselves or in an interaction with cue or outcome event, to predict memory in Experiment 1 (memory as a function of value estimate, β = −0.007, t = −0.15, p=0.88, interaction between event type and value estimate: β = −0.004, t = −0.06, p=0.95).
claims.evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2, value estimates were strongly correlated with the signed RPE at cue.
claims.source: In Experiment 2, the value estimates were strongly correlated with the signed RPE at cue (r > 0.80), therefore we could not enter them into a single model.
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, value estimates were trending in enhancing memory.
claims.source: When tested alone, value estimates were trending in enhancing memory in the instructed memory version of Experiment 2 (memory as a function of value estimate, β = 0.06, t = 1.89, p=0.06, interaction between event type and value estimate: β = 0.05, t = 1.19, p=0.24)
claims.evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis.

claims.claim: In the incidental memory version of Experiment 2, value estimates enhanced memory.
claims.source: and enhanced memory in the incidental memory version (memory as a function of value estimate, β = 0.08, t = 2.58, p=0.01, interaction between event type and value estimate: β = −0.03, t = −0.62, p=0.53).
claims.evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis.

claims.claim: The mnemonic modulation by value estimates is attributable to prediction errors rather than value estimates alone.
claims.source: However, given that value estimates did not influence memory when there was no prediction error at cue (Experiment 1), we believe the parsimonious interpretation is that this mnemonic modulation is attributable to prediction errors rather than value estimates alone.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from comparing results across experiments.

claims.claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, participants preferred both cues and outcomes associated with higher rewards.
claims.source: As expected, in the instructed memory version, participants preferred both cues and outcomes associated with higher rewards (mixed-effects logistic regression, choice as a function of reward difference: β = 1.59, z = 20.13, p<0.001; Figure 5A)
claims.evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of choice data.

claims.claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, participants preferred images for which they had reported higher subjective value when controlling for the effect of reward outcome on choice.
claims.source: and preferred images for which they had reported higher subjective value when controlling for the effect of reward outcome on choice (choice as a function of value difference: β = 0.92, z = 7.58, p<0.001; Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of choice data.

claims.claim: In the incidental memory version of Experiment 2, participants preferred images associated with higher rewards and higher subjective values, despite not being motivated to encode these associations.
claims.source: Interestingly, both effects were replicated in the incidental memory version of the task, despite not motivating participants to encode nor associate images with their values and reward outcomes (choice as a function of reward difference: β = 1.21, z = 12.28, p<0.001; Figure 5C; choice as a function of value difference, controlling for reward difference: β = 1.03, z = 7.84, p<0.001; Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of choice data.

claims.claim: In all experiments, participants were more likely to prefer the outcome event the more positive the outcome RPE, and to prefer the cue event the more negative the outcome RPE.
claims.source: In all experiments, we found that participants were more likely to prefer the outcome event the more positive the outcome RPE, and to prefer the cue event the more negative the outcome RPE (mixed-effects logistic regression, choice for outcome event as a function of signed outcome RPE, Experiment 1: β = 0.27, z = 3.27, p=0.001, Figure 6A; Experiment 2 - instructed memory: β = 0.23, z = 5.70, p<0.001, Figure 6B; Experiment 2 - incidental memory: β = 0.16, z = 4.30, p<0.001, Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of choice data across all experiments.

claims.claim: The preference effect of signed outcome RPE held when controlling for the magnitude of the outcome RPE.
claims.source: Moreover, each one of these effects held when controlling for the magnitude of the outcome RPE, that is the unsigned outcome RPE (which boosted memory for outcome images, see 'Unsigned but not signed reward prediction errors at outcome enhanced memory', above), thus suggesting this preference may not be driven by better memory for large RPE events.
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis controlling for confounding variables.

claims.claim: Unsigned RPEs at reward outcome modulated trial-specific learning rate, consistent with a Pearce-Hall model of learning.
claims.source: Drawing on classic associative models of attention (Pearce and Mackintosh, 2010), we found that an unsigned RPE at reward outcome modulated trial-specific learning rate, consistent with a Pearce-Hall model of learning that assumes more attention – and therefore more learning – for cues associated with unpredictable outcomes (Pearce and Hall, 1980).
claims.evidence: Supported by computational modeling results and citation to the Pearce-Hall model.

claims.claim: A signed RPE at reward cue modulated learning rate, consistent with a Mackintosh model of learning.
claims.source: Similarly, a signed RPE at reward cue also modulated learning rate, consistent with a Mackintosh, 1975 model of learning that assumes enhanced attention to reward-predicting cues.
claims.evidence: Supported by computational modeling results and citation to the Mackintosh model.

claims.claim: Reinforcement learning models that included both Pearce-Hall and Mackintosh modulatory components predicted behavior better than models without those attentional components.
claims.source: Reinforcement learning models that included both modulatory components predicted behavior better than models without those attentional components.
claims.evidence: Supported by model comparison results.

claims.claim: Unsigned RPEs at reward outcome improved memory for trial-unique scenes accompanying both the cue and outcome, most prominently the latter, in Experiment 1.
claims.source: We found that unsigned RPEs at reward outcome improved memory for trial-unique scenes accompanying both the cue and outcome, most prominently the latter.
claims.evidence: Supported by memory analysis results from Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Memory for the cue event increased with learning in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Unlike Experiment 1, where memory for the cue event remained relatively stable throughout the task, in Experiment 2, memory for the cue event (but not for the outcome event) increased with learning.
claims.evidence: Supported by memory analysis results comparing Experiments 1 and 2.

claims.claim: The mnemonic increase for cue events in Experiment 2 was supported by the gradual buildup of a signed RPE at cue.
claims.source: This mnemonic increase for cue events was supported by the gradual buildup of a signed RPE at cue, which enhanced memory for more valued reward cues, as well as an unsigned RPE at cue that benefited memory the more participants had separated the values of the two reward categories (i.e. the more they had learned).
claims.evidence: Supported by memory analysis results showing effects of both signed and unsigned cue RPEs.

claims.claim: Individual learning performance predicted the increase in cue memory over learning.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that individual learning performance predicted the increase in cue memory over learning, providing another link between stronger reward expectations and enhanced memory for cue events.
claims.evidence: Supported by individual differences analysis.

claims.claim: The mnemonic benefits of RPEs are not a result of strategic encoding.
claims.source: Importantly, our results were similar in both versions of Experiment 2, one that instructed memory for the images and their values and one where memory was completely incidental, confirming that the mnemonic benefits of RPEs are not a result of strategic encoding.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of results between instructed and incidental memory conditions.

claims.claim: Higher signed RPEs at outcome led to 'irrational' preference for the outcome event when choosing between cue and outcome scenes of a single trial.
claims.source: Additionally, when choosing between the cue and outcome scenes of a single trial (i.e. two scenes associated with the same reward and value), higher signed RPEs at outcome, which we did not find to modulate memory, nevertheless led to 'irrational' preference for the outcome event.
claims.evidence: Supported by choice analysis results.

claims.claim: Midbrain dopamine signals convey signed RPEs to target areas.
claims.source: As mentioned, one dominant hypothesis is that dopaminergic midbrain signals convey signed RPEs to target areas (Barto, 1995; Montague et al., 1996; Schultz et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on dopaminergic signaling.

claims.claim: Unsigned RPEs increase noradrenergic and dopaminergic firing from the locus coeruleus.
claims.source: Less well accepted, but also quite dominant is the idea that unsigned RPEs increase noradrenergic (as well as dopaminergic) firing from the LC (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Kempadoo et al., 2016; Wagatsuma et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on locus coeruleus function.

claims.claim: Midbrain dopamine initiates 'behavioral activation' which promotes the integration of higher-order representations, giving rise to semantic memories.
claims.source: Midbrain dopamine initiates 'behavioral activation' (Clewett and Murty, 2019), such as increased vigor during periods of reward anticipation (Niv et al., 2007), which is thought to promote the integration of higher-order representations, like value formation, giving rise to semantic memories (Duszkiewicz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dopamine and memory.

claims.claim: The LC-norepinephrine system promotes selectivity for salient events such as surprising outcomes, giving rise to distinctive, episodic memories.
claims.source: The LC-norepinephrine system, on the other hand, is thought to promote selectivity for salient events such as (positively or negatively) surprising outcomes, giving rise to distinctive, episodic memories (Duszkiewicz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on the LC-norepinephrine system and memory.

claims.claim: Phasic signed RPEs at cue would initiate and enhance a sustained period of reward anticipation, leading to memory benefits for ensuing events.
claims.source: However, based on our findings and the above mapping to neural substrates, we predict that phasic signed RPEs at cue would initiate and enhance a sustained (potentially ramping) period of reward anticipation, leading to memory benefits for ensuing events, regardless of their exact timepoint.
claims.evidence: Based on speculation and inference from the current findings and literature.

claims.claim: RPEs amplify anticipatory value according to a computational model by Iigaya and colleagues.
claims.source: Iigaya and colleagues recently offered such a computational model whereby RPEs amplify anticipatory value (i.e. the 'pleasure of savoring'; Iigaya et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claims.claim: The hippocampus enhances the functional coupling between the dopaminergic midbrain and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex to boost reward anticipation.
claims.source: They further suggested a neural circuit whereby the hippocampus – tracking unsigned RPEs at outcome – enhances the functional coupling between the dopaminergic midbrain (encoding the signed RPE at outcome) and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (encoding anticipatory value) to boost reward anticipation.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to neural circuit model.

claims.claim: More rewarding cues and more surprising outcomes were prioritized in memory, promoting adaptive behavior.
claims.source: In our experiments, we found a collaborative interaction between reinforcement learning and episodic memory systems: more rewarding cues and more surprising outcomes were prioritized in memory, thereby promoting adaptive behavior.
claims.evidence: Supported by the overall pattern of results from the experiments.

claims.claim: Compromised feedback-based learning has been associated with enhanced episodic memory in other paradigms.
claims.source: Nonetheless, in other paradigms, these two systems have been shown to compete for processing resources: compromised feedback-based learning has been associated with enhanced episodic memory, both behaviorally and neurally (Foerde et al., 2013; Wimmer et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature showing competition between learning and memory systems.

claims.claim: Better memory for reward-predicting cues was associated with weaker striatal RPEs at reward outcome in a study by Wimmer et al.
claims.source: In fact, Wimmer et al., 2014 showed that better memory for reward-predicting cues was associated with weaker striatal RPEs at reward outcome.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to specific study.

claims.claim: Participants were paid 10% of the rewards they received on every trial regardless of their estimates in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Participants were paid 10% of the rewards they received on every trial regardless of their estimates, in line with a Pavlovian conditioning environment.
claims.evidence: Describes the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: Participants were asked to make predictions to ensure they paid attention to outcomes in this passive-viewing, online task.
claims.source: Indeed, participants were asked to make predictions only to ensure they paid attention to outcomes in this passive-viewing, online task.
claims.evidence: Describes the rationale for the experimental design.

claims.claim: RPEs drive changes in emotional or affective states.
claims.source: This finding is consistent with work maintaining that RPEs drive changes in emotional or affective states (Villano et al., 2020; Eldar and Niv, 2015; Eldar et al., 2016; Rutledge et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on RPEs and affect.

claims.claim: The putative change in affect due to signed RPEs biased preference for the associated outcome event.
claims.source: and we propose that this putative change in affect biased preference for the associated outcome event.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the choice results and literature on affect.

claims.claim: Reward prediction errors generated by reward-predicting cues and reward outcomes modulate learning rate during reinforcement learning.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggest that reward prediction errors generated both by reward-predicting cues and by reward outcomes modulate learning rate during reinforcement learning, in line with classic attentional models of learning.
claims.evidence: Summary of main findings supported by data and citations.

claims.claim: RPE signals enhanced memory for events associated with larger unsigned prediction errors at outcome and larger signed prediction errors at cue.
claims.source: These signals further enhanced memory for events associated with larger unsigned prediction errors experienced at outcome (corresponding to general surprise), and larger signed prediction errors experienced at cue (corresponding to higher expected value).
claims.evidence: Summary of main findings supported by data.

claims.claim: The findings highlight the interaction of prediction errors with mnemonic processes, potentially signaled by midbrain dopamine and locus-coeruleus norepinephrine.
claims.source: These findings highlight the interaction of prediction errors, potentially signaled by midbrain dopamine and locus-coeruleus norepinephrine, with mnemonic processes.
claims.evidence: Summary statement connecting findings to neural mechanisms based on literature.

claims.claim: 100 participants were recruited for Experiment 1.
claims.source: We recruited participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk): Experiment 1: 100 participants
claims.evidence: Describes the sample size for the experiment.

claims.source: Experiment 2, instructed memory task: 400 participants (200 for each condition)
claims.evidence: Describes the sample size for the experiment.

claims.claim: 500 participants were recruited for Experiment 2, incidental memory task (250 for each condition).
claims.source: Experiment 2, incidental memory task: 500 participants (250 for each condition).
claims.evidence: Describes the sample size for the experiment.

claims.claim: The final sample included 81 participants in Experiment 1 after exclusions.
claims.source: This led to a final sample of 81 participants in Experiment 1

claims.claim: The final sample included 331 participants in Experiment 2, instructed memory task after exclusions.
claims.source: 331 participants in Experiment 2, instructed memory task (40¢−60¢ condition: 163, 20¢−80¢ condition: 168)

claims.claim: The final sample included 354 participants in Experiment 2, incidental memory task after exclusions.
claims.source: and 354 participants in Experiment 2, incidental memory task (40¢−60¢ condition: 168, 20¢−80¢ condition: 186).

claims.source: Participants were excluded if they (1) had a memory score of less than 0.5 (A': Sensitivity index in signal detection; Pollack and Norman, 1964)
claims.evidence: Describes exclusion criteria for the experiments.

claims.source: or (2) missed more than three trials.
claims.evidence: Describes exclusion criteria for the experiments.

claims.source: procedures were approved by Princeton University's Institutional Review Board.
claims.evidence: Describes ethical approval for the research.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, participants learned the average value of objects in two different reward contexts defined by background images of different cities ('Paris' and 'London').
claims.source: Participants learned the average value of objects in two different reward contexts, defined by background images of different cities ('Paris' and 'London').
claims.evidence: Describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, participants experienced each reward context in interleaved blocks (8 blocks total).
claims.source: They experienced each reward context in interleaved blocks (8 blocks total).
claims.evidence: Describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, each block was comprised of 6 or 9 trials (60 trials total).
claims.source: Each block was comprised of 6 or 9 trials (60 trials total)
claims.evidence: Describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1, each trial involved two trial-unique objects (120 objects in total).
claims.source: each trial involved two trial-unique objects (120 objects in total) that were randomly assigned to each trial.

results.result: Both unsigned RPEs at reward outcome and signed RPEs at reward cue dynamically modulate learning rate during reinforcement learning. Unsigned outcome RPEs boost learning rate (Pearce-Hall component), while signed cue RPEs anti-correlate with learning rate (Mackintosh component). Computational models including both components fit behavioral data better than models without these attentional components.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 provide direct statistical evidence for RPE modulation of learning rates. Claims C50-C52 and C18 demonstrate that computational models incorporating both Pearce-Hall and Mackintosh components significantly outperform simpler models via likelihood-ratio tests. Model recovery analysis (C99) validates that the data can distinguish between competing models. The convergence of empirical learning rate analysis and formal model comparison provides strong support.

results.result: Unsigned RPEs at reward outcome enhance memory for outcome images across all experiments, with effects driven by both reward variance and change points. This effect extends weakly to cue images in Experiment 1 but not Experiment 2. Signed outcome RPEs do not influence memory for either cue or outcome images.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 provide consistent statistical evidence across multiple experiments using both Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression. The null effect of signed outcome RPEs (C32) is well-powered and consistent with prior work (cited). The differential effects on cue vs. outcome memory are appropriately qualified and supported by interaction analyses. Effect sizes and confidence intervals are reported throughout.

results.result: Memory for cue events increases with learning in Experiment 2 but not Experiment 1. This increase is supported by signed cue RPEs (enhancing memory for higher-value cues) and unsigned cue RPEs (reflecting learned value separation). Individual learning performance predicts the magnitude of cue memory increase, particularly in the incidental memory condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 establish the differential pattern across experiments with appropriate statistical controls. Claims C33-C37 demonstrate the mechanistic contributions of both signed and unsigned cue RPEs with Bayesian and frequentist analyses. The individual differences analysis (C26-C27) provides converging evidence linking learning to memory enhancement. The failure to find effects in the 40¢-60¢ incidental condition (C24) is appropriately explained by worse learning performance in that condition.

results.result: High reward variance in Experiment 1 produced an interaction effect on memory: lower memory for cue events and higher memory for outcome events compared to low variance conditions, with the effect significant for outcome events but not cue events.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21 report a significant interaction with appropriate statistical testing. However, the interpretation is somewhat limited as the within-interaction effects show significance only for outcome events. The result is consistent with the unsigned outcome RPE findings but the asymmetry between cue and outcome effects within the interaction warrants caution in interpretation.

results.result: Participants showed better value learning in the easier 20¢-80¢ condition compared to the 40¢-60¢ condition, and better learning in the instructed memory version compared to the incidental memory version. Participants tested during the pandemic showed more pessimistic reward expectations overall.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 report straightforward manipulation checks and descriptive findings with appropriate statistical support. The pandemic effect (C16) is interesting but somewhat tangential to the main hypotheses. These results establish that the experimental manipulations worked as intended and document important differences between conditions that inform interpretation of memory results.

results.result: Reward outcomes and value estimates alone did not predict memory when controlling for RPEs. In Experiment 2, value estimates were highly correlated with signed cue RPEs (r > 0.80) and showed trending or significant effects on memory, but these effects are attributable to prediction errors rather than values alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 provide appropriate control analyses demonstrating that RPE effects are not simply driven by reward magnitude or value. The high correlation between value estimates and cue RPEs (C40) is acknowledged and appropriately handled. The inference that effects are due to RPEs rather than values (C43) is supported by the null result in Experiment 1 where cue RPEs were absent. This strengthens the main RPE findings.

results.result: In choice tests, participants preferred images associated with higher rewards and values in both instructed and incidental memory conditions. When choosing between cue and outcome images from the same trial (same reward/value), signed outcome RPEs biased preference toward outcome events, an effect that persisted when controlling for unsigned RPEs and may reflect affective changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 demonstrate robust preference effects with appropriate statistical modeling. The 'irrational' preference effect (C58) is well-controlled and provides novel insight into signed RPE effects on preference despite null memory effects. The affective interpretation (C72) is appropriately qualified as speculative but is supported by citations. The choice data provide converging evidence for value learning and reveal dissociations between memory and preference.

results.result: The mnemonic benefits of RPEs are not due to strategic encoding, as similar results were obtained in both instructed and incidental memory conditions. The findings demonstrate a collaborative interaction between reinforcement learning and episodic memory systems, with more rewarding cues and surprising outcomes prioritized in memory.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by the replication of key effects across instructed and incidental memory conditions, though some differences exist (e.g., C33 vs C34). Claim C66 appropriately synthesizes the overall pattern of results. The conclusion about non-strategic encoding is strengthened by the incidental memory condition, though the instructed condition showed some differences in learning (C15) that complicate interpretation.

results.result: The manuscript reviews established neuroscientific knowledge about RPE signaling: dopaminergic systems convey signed RPEs and modulate hippocampal plasticity, while the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system responds to unsigned RPEs and co-releases dopamine to the hippocampus. These systems are proposed to support different memory processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C8 and C59-C62 accurately cite established literature on dopaminergic and noradrenergic signaling. The citations are appropriate and the characterizations are consistent with the cited work. These claims provide the theoretical framework for interpreting the behavioral findings but do not constitute novel empirical results from this study.

results.result: The authors predict that phasic signed RPEs at cue would initiate sustained reward anticipation leading to memory benefits for subsequent events, drawing on computational models and neural circuit proposals from prior work.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is explicitly speculative and not tested in the current experiments. Claims C64-C65 accurately cite prior computational and neural circuit models but these are not validated here. While the speculation is reasonable given the findings, it remains untested and represents future work rather than a supported result from the current data.

results.result: Prior work has shown that reinforcement learning and memory systems can compete, with compromised feedback-based learning associated with enhanced episodic memory, contrasting with the collaborative interaction found in the current experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 accurately cite prior literature showing competition between learning and memory systems. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current collaborative findings but do not represent results from the current study. The citations are appropriate and the characterization is accurate.

results.result: The study recruited 100 participants for Experiment 1, 400 for Experiment 2 instructed memory, and 500 for Experiment 2 incidental memory from Amazon Mechanical Turk. After applying exclusion criteria (memory score < 0.5 or >3 missed trials), final samples were 81, 331, and 354 participants respectively. Procedures were IRB-approved.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 provide straightforward methodological details about sample sizes, exclusions, and ethical approval. The exclusion criteria are reasonable and clearly stated. Sample sizes appear adequate based on the reported power analysis (C76). These are standard methodological details that are appropriately documented.

results.result: The manuscript describes the experimental designs for Experiments 1 and 2, including trial structure, reward distributions, variance manipulations, memory tests, and choice tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C96 provide detailed methodological descriptions of the experimental procedures. These are clearly stated and internally consistent. The designs are appropriate for testing the stated hypotheses about RPE effects on learning and memory. These are standard methodological details necessary for reproducibility.

results.result: The study employed appropriate computational modeling (Rescorla-Wagner variants), statistical analysis (mixed-effects models), and Bayesian hierarchical modeling approaches. Model recovery analysis validated that the data could distinguish between competing models.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 describe the analytical approaches used. The methods are appropriate and well-established. Model recovery (C99) is a critical validation that strengthens confidence in model comparison results. The combination of frequentist and Bayesian approaches provides complementary perspectives. These methodological choices are sound and well-justified.

results.result: Participants in Experiment 1 were paid 10% of rewards regardless of estimate accuracy to create a Pavlovian environment. Predictions were requested to ensure attention. The choice preference effects are consistent with RPEs driving affective state changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 describe design rationale that is reasonable and clearly stated. Claim C71 cites appropriate literature on RPEs and affect. These claims provide context for interpreting the Pavlovian learning paradigm and choice results, though C71's affective interpretation is somewhat speculative.

results.result: Prior work by the authors and others found that unsigned RPEs at outcome boost learning and memory, while signed RPEs at cue enhance memory, providing the foundation for the current hypotheses.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 accurately cite prior literature including the authors' own work and related studies. These citations appropriately motivate the current experiments and hypotheses. The characterization of prior findings is accurate based on the cited sources.

results.result: The study demonstrates that both signed and unsigned RPEs enhance memory, potentially through midbrain dopamine and locus coeruleus norepinephrine modulation of hippocampal plasticity, reconciling separate findings in the literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C75 represent high-level summary statements of the main findings. These are well-supported by the detailed results (C28-C37) and appropriately qualified regarding neural mechanisms ('potentially'). The claim to reconcile prior literature is reasonable given the demonstration of both signed and unsigned RPE effects in a single paradigm, though the neural mechanisms are inferred rather than directly tested.
